# Market and competitor research

## Goal
Understand how competitors use content to attract the audience we care about, what appears to work for them, and where our website can make a useful contribution. This is primarily SEO and content research, not a general product-feature comparison. Market context helps interpret the content strategy, but should not displace analysis of published pages.

## Suggested approach
Start with existing business context, research and the decision this work should support. Identify direct competitors and sites competing for the same search attention, including publishers and communities without competing products. Explain the research plan, investigate in a useful batch, then return with findings and a small group of questions where owner input would help.

Prioritize blogs and other search-oriented content: guides, tutorials, comparison and alternatives pages, templates, tools and topic hubs. Explore blog indexes, categories, sitemaps and representative articles. Notice recurring topics, intended readers, questions, formats, depth, publication/update patterns, internal links and calls to action. Visible dates and listings can be incomplete; explain sample coverage.

Read the posts themselves to understand what the competitor seems to be trying to achieve. Beginner guides may suggest category education; alternatives pages may target people considering a switch; templates may attract people ready to implement. These are interpretations of editorial intent, not proof of success. Product or pricing pages help explain how content connects to the offer, rather than becoming the main subject of research.

If Ahrefs, Semrush or a comparable provider is available, investigate ranking keywords and top-performing organic pages. Keep keywords, ranking URLs, positions, country/database, observation date and available volume/traffic estimates connected. Define 'top-performing', for example by estimated organic traffic, rather than implying knowledge of conversions or revenue. Use comparable filters across sites and retain provider limitations.

Without those tools, public posts still reveal targeting, topic clusters, formats and likely visitor journeys. Do not call sampled pages top performers merely because they are prominent or recent. Distinguish provider estimates or observed rankings from inferred keyword targets. Publishing on a topic does not by itself validate demand for our own page.

Compare their approach with our existing content and expertise. Look for relevant coverage gaps, weak or outdated answers, useful formats and questions we can answer with stronger examples or proof. Recommend what to investigate, improve or create, not copying their calendar wholesale. Refine findings through owner feedback without requiring every question answered on day one.

## Tools and integrations
Prefer available search and page-reading tools such as Composio web search and Context.dev. Use discovery/configuration capabilities when available to find suitable search, scraping or SEO data tools and enable them within authorized scope. Reuse ready connections; request authentication only where needed. Ahrefs and Semrush are options, not claims of connected access. Supplied exports can also help when their source, scope and date are known.

Browser or direct HTTP can fill retrieval gaps. General web search supports discovery but is not a localized Google ranking capture unless it actually provides that evidence. Ask about private research the owner is willing to share when it would improve interpretation.

## Useful output
An explanation of competitors' SEO and content strategies, supported by representative posts and available keyword/top-page data. Show the audiences and intents they seem to target, what is demonstrably performing versus inferred, and implications for our next decisions. Profiles, page inventories, topic maps or comparison tables should serve that explanation.

## Organizing inputs and outputs
Read canonical context from agent-files/00-context/ and existing research from agent-files/01-research/. For app-owned work, follow linked records in agent-files/apps/seo-workspace/knowledge/, inputs/ and discoveries/. Inputs include competitor domains, the research question, prior findings and available exports.

Reuse the canonical competitor research folder, currently agent-files/01-research/competitor-map/, with dated investigation subfolders. Save original page captures and provider responses/exports in raw/ beside the analysis, retaining URL, retrieval date, locale, filters and units. A page inventory can connect each domain, URL, topic, inferred intent and metrics without forcing a fixed report template. Preserve earlier snapshots for future comparisons.

Save the synthesis in the existing app Discovery when it owns the work; otherwise keep it in the durable research folder. Link the synthesis to raw evidence and relevant Knowledge. Update existing competitor notes instead of creating duplicate active profiles. Any durable recovery copy of app-owned work is labeled an archive, not a second editable record. Update agent-files/INDEX.md so planning and briefing can find the result.

## Scope
The focus is competitors' search and content activity. Detailed product trials, backlink campaigns, article writing and monitoring are separate work when requested.
